questions.q: What is the single sentence that distinguishes real Snowpark usage from "I used a Python connector to pull data into pandas"?
options: Snowpark only works with CSV files, not Snowflake tables
Snowpark code is translated and pushed down to run inside Snowflake's own engine, so the data never leaves Snowflake
Snowpark is faster because it runs entirely on your local machine
Snowpark replaces SQL entirely, so you never need to know SQL
questions.explain: Snowpark's defining property is that the computation itself executes inside Snowflake, governed by the same RBAC and billing as any query -- it doesn't move data out to a separate Python process.

questions.q: Which of these is a Snowpark DataFrame transformation (builds the query plan only, runs nothing yet)?
options: collect()
show()
filter()
count()
questions.explain: filter(), select(), group_by(), and agg() are transformations -- they only build the query plan. collect(), count(), and show() are all actions that actually execute the query.

questions.q: Given `df = session.table("orders").filter(col("status") == "refunded")`, has any query executed against Snowflake by this line?
options: It depends on the size of the orders table
Yes -- session.table() always executes immediately
Yes -- filter() always triggers execution
No -- filter() only builds a query plan; nothing runs until an action like collect() is called
questions.explain: Both session.table() and filter() are lazy -- the DataFrame only represents a plan until an action method is called.

questions.q: What does calling both df.count() and then df.collect() on the same DataFrame actually do, mechanically?
options: Causes an error, since a DataFrame can only call one action
Runs the underlying query twice -- each action is its own separate round trip to Snowflake
Only the first action call actually executes anything
Runs the query once and caches the result automatically for both calls
questions.explain: Each action is independently a new round trip to Snowflake -- calling multiple actions on the same DataFrame re-runs the query each time unless you explicitly cache the result yourself.

questions.q: What naming convention does the real Snowpark Python API use for its DataFrame methods?
options: PascalCase, e.g. GroupBy()
camelCase, e.g. groupBy() -- identical to Spark's Scala API
All uppercase, e.g. GROUP_BY()
snake_case, e.g. group_by() -- not camelCase like groupBy()
questions.explain: Snowpark's Python API uses snake_case (group_by, with_column, etc.) -- a detail worth getting right since it visually resembles, but differs from, Spark's camelCase DataFrame API.
